final.title: Why testimonial consent is not enough
final.body:
If you ever want to use a story about a pilot or a result, consent is only one check. It answers who agreed to be quoted. It does not answer the harder question: does the wording still stay inside what was actually done, and does it avoid implying capability, scale, or impact you have not shown?

That distinction matters in a small business. A quote can be perfectly real and still be misleading if it starts sounding like proof of a finished system, a guaranteed ROI, or a broader deployment than you can support. Consent is not evidence. It is permission.

The practical next step is simple: before any story is published, write down three items in plain English — what was done, what the person agreed could be said, and what claims are off limits. Then check the draft against that list line by line. If a sentence reads like a promise, it needs another pass. Human approval stays in the loop before anything goes public. That is less exciting than marketing magic, but it keeps the claim honest.

final.title: Why testimonial consent is not enough
final.body:
If you ever plan to use a customer story, consent is only one check. It answers who agreed to be quoted. It does not answer whether the story is accurate, whether it is being used in the right scope, or whether it quietly suggests capabilities you have not actually shown.

That matters for a small business because a testimonial can drift into a promise. A person may approve a quote and still not be approving every channel, every edit, or every implied result. And if the wording makes a pilot sound like a finished system, you have crossed from evidence into marketing spin. That is a bad trade, even if it is tidy prose.

The practical next step is simple: before any story is published, write down three items in plain English — what was actually done, what the person agreed could be said, and what claims are off limits. Then read the final wording against those three lines. If it sounds like a guarantee, or if it implies scale, ROI, or deployment that you cannot verify, it needs another pass.

Human approval should stay in the loop before anything goes public.
